query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, phase stability and the resultant suite of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness are governed by a critical level of chemical ordering induced by aluminum. This ordering, which promotes the formation of a duplex (lamellar) microstructure comprising a soft FCC matrix interleaved with a hard, ordered B2 phase, stabilizes the microstructure under diverse service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy (or compositions near this ratio) exhibiting a dual-phase FCC/B2 lamellar structure.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the aluminum content (and possibly its distribution via controlled thermo-mechanical processing) around the eutectic composition while keeping the other elemental ratios nearly constant.
generation.conditions: Samples to be tested under high-temperature exposure, corrosive environments (e.g., chloride-containing acid solutions), radiation or simulated defect injection, and cryogenic tensile tests.
generation.structural_mediator: The lamellar microstructure—specifically, the coexistence and spatial arrangement of the FCC phase with a chemically ordered B2 phase.
generation.mechanism: An aluminum content above a critical threshold enhances chemical ordering, which drives the formation of an interpenetrating duplex microstructure. The internal phase boundaries act as barriers to defect propagation (improving radiation tolerance), slow down oxide growth/corrosion processes (enhancing environmental resistance), and provide a balanced distribution of soft and hard regions (ensuring high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline eutectic alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1), alloys with optimized (slightly higher) Al content will show a more pronounced and stable lamellar FCC/B2 structure that retains its phase integrity and mechanical properties over the tested conditions. In contrast, alloys with lower or excessively high Al content will either not develop the dual-phase structure or will form excessive ordered phases leading to embrittlement, respectively.
generation.baseline: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy with established eutectic FCC/B2 lamellar microstructure displaying a balanced combination of strength, ductility, and corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is constrained to compositional ranges typical of eutectic HEAs. Outside this range, where the elemental ratios deviate significantly from the eutectic point, other phase formations (e.g., single-phase solid solutions or intermetallic compounds) may dominate, and the mechanism of aluminum‐induced ordering may not govern phase stability.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative threshold of aluminum that optimizes chemical ordering is uncertain, as is the relative contribution of other processing conditions (e.g., cooling rate, thermo-mechanical treatment) on phase stability. Additionally, while the hypothesis is supported by observed lamellar microstructures in previous studies, the direct link to radiation tolerance and cryogenic behavior requires further systematic exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy samples with systematically varied aluminum content around the eutectic composition. Subject samples to identical thermo-mechanical processing to establish comparable initial microstructures, then expose them to high-temperature corrosion tests, simulated radiation damage (or defect injection tests), and cryogenic tensile testing. Use advanced microscopy (e.g., TEM, XRD) to evaluate the dual-phase (FCC/B2) structure before and after exposures.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification (FCC versus B2 volume fractions) via XRD and TEM.
Mechanical properties (tensile strength, yield strength, ductility) measured at room, high, and cryogenic temperatures.
Environmental/corrosion resistance via potentiodynamic polarization tests.
Defect evolution or radiation tolerance metrics (e.g., displacement per atom, retention of ductility) from simulated radiation experiments.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If varying the aluminum content within the tested range does not result in significant differences in the formation or stability of the dual-phase lamellar structure, or if improved chemical ordering (as measured by the degree of B2 phase formation) does not correlate with enhanced high-temperature strength, corrosion resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline composition, then the hypothesis that aluminum-induced chemical ordering drives phase stability for these desirable properties is falsified.

A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata

Abstract: AbstractTogether with the thermodynamics and kinetics, the complex microstructure of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) exerts a significant influence on the associated oxidation mechanisms in these concentrated solid solutions. To describe the surface oxidation in AlCoCrFeNi HEA, we employed a stochastic cellular automata model that replicates the mesoscale structures that form. The model benefits from diffusion coefficients of the principal elements through the native oxides predicted by using molecular simulations. Through our examination of the oxidation behavior as a function of the alloy composition, we corroborated that the oxide scale growth is a function of the complex chemistry and resultant microstructures. The effect of heat treatment on these alloys is also simulated by using reconstructed experimental micrographs. When they are in a single-crystal structure, no segregation is noted for α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3, which are the primary scale-forming oxides.
